etymology: A 2024 exclamation of surprise or disgust that spread through TikTok and "brainrot" videos, formed by dropping the meme-word sigma (from the manosphere’s "sigma male") into the slot of a familiar profane phrase. It is a minced oath — a swap that lets a child say the shape of a curse without the curse word — and Gen Alpha uses it constantly and ironically, alongside skibidi and Ohio, for anything weird.
biblical_def: "What the sigma?" is what a Gen Alpha kid says when something is surprising, weird, or gross. It sounds silly, and it is — but it is built on the frame of a swear phrase, with "sigma" dropped in where the bad word goes. The Christian observation: Scripture cares not only about which words we say but about what our words are doing. Jesus said, "let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay: for whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil" (Mat 5:37). Paul ruled out "filthiness, nor foolish talking, nor jesting, which are not convenient: but rather giving of thanks" (Eph 5:4). A minced oath is a way of keeping the swear without saying it — the heart wants the curse, the mouth changes one word. That is why many Christian families have always been careful with "gosh" and "darn" too: not because the substitute is wicked, but because it keeps a profane habit warm. The better goal is speech "alway with grace, seasoned with salt" (Col 4:6). A father can tell a five-year-old: "‘What the sigma’ is a silly way of saying a not-nice phrase. Let’s say ‘Whoa!’ or ‘Wow!’ instead — God made lots of good words for being surprised."
webster_summary: 2024 minced-oath exclamation with meme-word sigma in a swear phrase’s slot — silly on its face, built to keep the shape of a curse that Scripture would have us leave.
webster_full: WHAT THE SIGMA, interj. (Gen Alpha slang, 2024–present) An exclamation of surprise, confusion, or disgust. "What the sigma is that?"
Formed on the pattern of a profane phrase, with sigma substituted — a minced oath.
Companions: skibidi, Ohio, rizz, gyatt.
Decode for parents: mild, but it carries a curse’s frame; offer a clean replacement.
scriptures: Mat 5:37
But let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay: for whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil.
Eph 5:4
Neither filthiness, nor foolish talking, nor jesting, which are not convenient: but rather giving of thanks.
Col 4:6
Let your speech be alway with grace, seasoned with salt, that ye may know how ye ought to answer every man.
Jas 5:12
But above all things, my brethren, swear not, neither by heaven, neither by the earth, neither by any other oath: but let your yea be yea; and your nay, nay; lest ye fall into condemnation.
corruption_summary: What the sigma keeps the frame of a profane phrase with a meme-word swapped in; Scripture asks for yea-and-nay speech seasoned with grace, not a curse in disguise.
corruption_paragraphs: Minced oaths are old — "gosh," "golly," "heck" — and Christians have long debated them. The modern version is more transparent: children know exactly which word "sigma" replaces, and the joke is the near-miss. The habit trains the tongue to reach for a curse’s shape whenever something startles.

Treat it lightly but deliberately. Do not panic; do offer better words. Teach Col 4:6 as the goal, and make surprise words fun: "Whoa!" "No way!" "Praise God!" Children copy what is said with gusto at home.
roots_summary: Manosphere sigma (via "sigma male") inserted into a profane phrase → "what the sigma" (TikTok, 2024) → Gen Alpha exclamation.
roots_lines: Greek letter sigma → manosphere "sigma male" (2010s)
2020s: sigma as a general meme-word for cool or weird
2024: "what the sigma" on TikTok and in brainrot videos
Pattern: minced oath — a mild word in a curse’s slot
usage: "What the sigma, there’s a frog in the pool!"
Let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay (Mat 5:37).
Speech alway with grace, seasoned with salt — not with sigma (Col 4:6).

etymology: A stone-faced, jaw-clenched, eyes-narrowed expression — sometimes with one raised eyebrow — imitated from "sigma edits" of brooding film characters (Patrick Bateman of American Psycho, 2000; Thomas Shelby of Peaky Blinders; Ryan Gosling’s driver in Drive, 2011) and from the raised-eyebrow "Rock" meme. From about 2021 Gen Alpha boys began making the sigma face for photos, in class, and on command, as a pose of cool superiority.
biblical_def: The sigma face is the cold, serious stare a Gen Alpha kid makes to look tough — jaw tight, eyes squinted, no smile. Boys do it for pictures and mirror it from videos of movie characters. The Christian observation: a face is never only a face; Scripture treats the face as a window of the heart. "A merry heart maketh a cheerful countenance" (Pro 15:13); "As in water face answereth to face, so the heart of man to man" (Pro 27:19). The sigma face is a mask of coldness, and many of the characters it is copied from are cold for terrible reasons — one of the most-edited is a fictional serial killer. Jesus warned against faces put on for an audience: the hypocrites "disfigure their faces, that they may appear unto men" (Mat 6:16). And Scripture’s highest picture of a face is a warm one: "The LORD make his face shine upon thee, and be gracious unto thee" (Num 6:25). God’s face toward His children is not a sigma stare; it shines. A father can tell a five-year-old: "You don’t have to make a mean face to be strong. God’s face shines at you with love — let’s practice our shining faces!" And he can quietly find out which edits his son is copying the face from.
webster_summary: The cold, jaw-clenched pose copied from "sigma edits" of brooding film men (c. 2021-) — a mask of superiority, against the shining face of the LORD and the cheerful countenance of a merry heart.
webster_full: SIGMA FACE, n. (Gen Alpha slang, c. 2021–present) A stern, emotionless, jaw-clenched expression, often with a raised eyebrow, imitating "sigma" film characters. "Do the sigma face for the picture."
Sources: sigma edits of Patrick Bateman, Thomas Shelby, and similar characters; the raised-eyebrow "Rock" meme.
Related: mewing, mogging, jawline, hunter eyes.
Decode for parents: the pose is harmless; the characters it imitates often are not.
scriptures: A merry heart maketh a cheerful countenance: but by sorrow of the heart the spirit is broken.
As in water face answereth to face, so the heart of man to man.
Mat 6:16
Moreover when ye fast, be not, as the hypocrites, of a sad countenance: for they disfigure their faces, that they may appear unto men to fast. Verily I say unto you, They have their reward.
Num 6:25
The LORD make his face shine upon thee, and be gracious unto thee:
corruption_summary: The sigma face is coldness worn as a costume, copied from men who are often cold because they are cruel; Scripture reads the face as the heart’s mirror and lifts up the shining face of God.
corruption_paragraphs: Boys have always practiced tough faces in mirrors. What is new is the source: algorithm-fed edits that glorify cruelty set to dramatic music, so that the face of a fictional killer becomes the model of manhood for ten-year-olds. The pose trains a boy to equate strength with emotional deadness and superiority with contempt.

Correct gently and give a better picture. Christ’s strength was never cold; He wept, rejoiced, rebuked, and embraced. Tell your son the strongest Man who ever lived had a face that children ran toward. Then let him laugh in the photo.
roots_summary: Manosphere sigma + English face → sigma edits of brooding film men (c. 2020–21) → the posed "sigma face" (Gen Alpha).
roots_lines: Latin facies — form, face, countenance → English face
2010s: manosphere "sigma male" archetype
c. 2020–21: sigma edits of Patrick Bateman, Thomas Shelby, and others
Gen Alpha: the sigma face as a photo pose
usage: "Why is everyone in the class picture doing the sigma face?"
As in water face answereth to face, so the heart (Pro 27:19).
The LORD make his face shine upon thee — no sigma stare in heaven (Num 6:25).

etymology: An older English idiom (early twentieth century) for a person who prefers to act alone, from the wolf separated from its pack. In the 2010s–2020s manosphere and meme culture, the lone wolf became the badge of the "sigma" — the self-sufficient outsider who needs no one — and wolf-howling-at-the-moon images captioned with solitary-strength slogans circulated widely; Gen Alpha boys absorbed the phrase as a compliment: "I’m a lone wolf."
biblical_def: To call yourself a lone wolf in Gen Alpha talk is to say you don’t need anybody — you’re tough, independent, cooler on your own. The meme comes with pictures of wolves howling at the moon. The Christian observation: Scripture says the opposite about the wolf and the opposite about being alone. The first thing in creation God called "not good" was loneliness: "It is not good that the man should be alone" (Gen 2:18). "Two are better than one... For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow: but woe to him that is alone when he falleth" (Ecc 4:9-10). Christians are told not to forsake "the assembling of ourselves together" (Heb 10:25). And in the Bible the wolf is not the hero; it is the predator that scatters the flock. God’s people are sheep, and that is good news, because sheep have a Shepherd: "I am the good shepherd: the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep" (Joh 10:11). A father can tell a five-year-old: "Wolves are cool animals, but God says it’s not good to be alone. We’re more like sheep — and Jesus is our Shepherd who takes care of us, with our family and our church." A boy who wants to be strong can learn that the strongest men in Scripture had brothers.
webster_summary: Early-20th-c. idiom for a solitary actor, made a "sigma" badge by meme culture — the self-sufficiency Scripture calls not good, and the predator the Good Shepherd guards His sheep against.
webster_full: LONE WOLF, n. (English idiom, early 20th c.; meme and Gen Alpha usage, 2010s–present) One who prefers to act alone; in meme culture, a self-sufficient "sigma" outsider. "I don’t need a team. Lone wolf."
Meme form: a wolf howling at the moon, captioned with solitary-strength slogans.
Older and darker sense: a lone attacker acting without a group.
Decode for parents: sometimes a cover for loneliness; ask gently.
Webster 1828, the root — WOLF, n. An animal of the genus Canis, a beast of prey that kills sheep and other small domestic animals; called sometimes the wild dog.
Webster 1828, the root — LONE, a. Solitary; retired; unfrequented; having no company.
scriptures: Gen 2:18
And the LORD God said, It is not good that the man should be alone; I will make him an help meet for him.
Ecc 4:9
Two are better than one; because they have a good reward for their labour.
Ecc 4:10
For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow: but woe to him that is alone when he falleth; for he hath not another to help him up.
Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as the manner of some is; but exhorting one another: and so much the more, as ye see the day approaching.
I am the good shepherd: the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep.
corruption_summary: The lone-wolf ideal crowns isolation as strength; Scripture calls aloneness not good, casts the wolf as the flock’s enemy, and gives the sheep a Shepherd and a fold.
corruption_paragraphs: The meme flatters a real wound. Many boys feel alone, and the lone-wolf image turns that pain into a pose: I am not lonely, I am above needing anyone. It is pride guarding loneliness, and it leaves the boy more alone. The manosphere uses the same image to sell a manhood of self-sufficiency that Scripture never knew.

Answer with fellowship. Put your son beside other boys and men — a church, a team, a father who spends time. Teach Ecclesiastes 4 and John 10. The wolf is not the Bible’s hero; the Shepherd is, and He makes the lonely part of a flock.
roots_summary: Old English wulf + lone → idiom lone wolf (early 20th c.) → manosphere "sigma" badge (2010s) → Gen Alpha boast.
roots_lines: Old English wulf; lone, clipped from alone
Early 20th c.: lone wolf, a solitary person
2010s: manosphere sigma archetype; wolf-moon meme images
Gen Alpha: "I’m a lone wolf" as compliment
usage: "I’m doing the project by myself. Lone wolf." "Two are better than one, bud."
It is not good that the man should be alone (Gen 2:18).
The wolf scatters the sheep; the good Shepherd gives his life for them (Joh 10:11-12).

etymology: From a 2022–23 meme in which young men posted images of brooding, lonely, often violent film characters — Ryan Gosling’s driver in Drive (2011) and K in Blade Runner 2049 (2017), the Joker (2019), Patrick Bateman, Travis Bickle of Taxi Driver (1976) — with the caption "literally me." The "literally me" characters became a recognized list. Gen Alpha uses the phrase more broadly and lightly — "this sleepy cat is literally me" — but the brooding-hero sense lives on in edits.
biblical_def: "Literally me" means "that’s exactly like me" — said about a character, an animal video, or a meme. Gen Alpha kids say it about anything relatable, and older boys say it about a set of lonely, angry movie men. The Christian observation: the phrase is about identification — who do I see myself in? — and that is one of the most important questions a child ever answers. Scripture says a believer is being shaped into one image above all: God’s people are "predestinate to be conformed to the image of his Son" (Rom 8:29). Paul could say, "Be ye followers of me, even as I also am of Christ" (1Co 11:1), because he was looking at Jesus. The "literally me" heroes are mostly men who are lonely, bitter, and violent, and the Psalm warns about walking in their counsel: "Blessed is the man that walketh not in the counsel of the ungodly, nor standeth in the way of sinners" (Psa 1:1). Whom a boy calls "literally me" he is likely to become. The better answer is "looking unto Jesus the author and finisher of our faith" (Heb 12:2). A father can tell a five-year-old: "It’s fun when a cartoon is just like us! But the best one to be like is Jesus — and God is making us more like Him every day."
webster_summary: Meme caption (2022–23) identifying with brooding film men, now any relatable thing — a question of identification, answered by the image of the Son into which believers are conformed.
webster_full: LITERALLY ME, phr. (internet meme, 2022–present; Gen Alpha usage) "That is exactly like me"; said of a character, image, or video. "This hamster stuffing his face is literally me."
Meme canon: the "literally me" characters — Gosling’s driver and K, the Joker, Patrick Bateman, Travis Bickle, Tyler Durden.
Decode for parents: light in a child’s mouth, heavier in a teen’s; notice which characters.
scriptures: Rom 8:29
For whom he did foreknow, he also did predestinate to be conformed to the image of his Son, that he might be the firstborn among many brethren.
Be ye followers of me, even as I also am of Christ.
Psa 1:1
Blessed is the man that walketh not in the counsel of the ungodly, nor standeth in the way of sinners, nor sitteth in the seat of the scornful.
Heb 12:2
Looking unto Jesus the author and finisher of our faith; who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising the shame, and is set down at the right hand of the throne of God.
corruption_summary: "Literally me" teaches young men to find themselves in lonely, bitter, violent heroes; Scripture says the believer is being conformed to the image of Christ and calls him to look unto Jesus.
corruption_paragraphs: Identification is formation. The "literally me" canon is a gallery of isolated, wounded, often murderous men, presented with sympathy and style. A teenage boy who sees himself in them is being offered a story about his loneliness: that it makes him special, that his anger is justified, that he is the misunderstood hero. That story has ended badly in real life.

Give your son better mirrors. Tell him the stories of David, Daniel, Nehemiah, and above all Christ, and of real men you know who are faithful. Ask him who he thinks is "literally him" and listen. Then tell him the truth Rom 8:29 holds out: God intends him to look like Jesus.
roots_summary: English literally (intensifier) + me → "literally me" meme canon (2022–23) → general Gen Alpha relatable-caption.
roots_lines: Latin littera (letter) → literally, now an intensifier
2022–23: "literally me" posts of brooding film characters
Canon: Drive (2011), Blade Runner 2049 (2017), Joker (2019), American Psycho, Taxi Driver
Gen Alpha: any relatable image is "literally me"
usage: "That cat falling asleep in the cereal bowl is literally me."
Conformed to the image of his Son — that’s who you’re becoming (Rom 8:29).
Be ye followers of me, even as I also am of Christ (1Co 11:1).

etymology: From the Japanese manga Jujutsu Kaisen (Gege Akutami), chapter 221 (2023): asked whether he would lose to the demon king Sukuna, the sorcerer Gojo Satoru answers, "Nah, I’d win." Fifteen chapters later, in September 2023, Gojo is killed in that fight. The line became a meme of supreme confidence — posted beside impossible matchups — and, after Gojo’s death, of confidence about to be humbled. Gen Alpha says it about any challenge.
biblical_def: "Nah, I’d win" is what you say when someone asks if you could lose — "Could you beat a gorilla?" "Nah, I’d win." It comes from an anime hero who said it right before he lost badly. The Christian observation: the meme is funny precisely because Scripture’s law is true — the boast before the fight is the boast that falls. "Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall" (Pro 16:18). An Israelite king gave the perfect answer to an enemy’s boast: "Let not him that girdeth on his harness boast himself as he that putteth it off" (1Ki 20:11) — don’t brag putting your armor on, only taking it off. Paul warns, "let him that thinketh he standeth take heed lest he fall" (1Co 10:12), and James teaches the humble way to talk about tomorrow: "ye ought to say, If the Lord will, we shall live, and do this, or that" (Jas 4:15). There is a right confidence, and David had it before Goliath — but his was in God: "the battle is the LORD’s" (1Sa 17:47). A father can tell a five-year-old: "It’s good to be brave. But we don’t brag that we’ll win. We say, ‘With God’s help, I’ll do my best!’ — and God is the One who really wins."
webster_summary: Gojo Satoru’s boast in Jujutsu Kaisen (2023), shortly before his defeat — a meme of overconfidence that proves Proverbs: pride goeth before destruction.
webster_full: NAH, I’D WIN, phr. (manga meme, 2023–present; Gen Alpha usage) A boast of confidence in an impossible matchup. "Could you beat a hundred men?" "Nah, I’d win."
Source: Gojo Satoru, Jujutsu Kaisen chapter 221 (2023); his defeat followed in chapter 236.
Decode for parents: usually a joke about overconfidence; a ready lesson in Proverbs 16:18.
scriptures: Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall.
And the king of Israel answered and said, Tell him, Let not him that girdeth on his harness boast himself as he that putteth it off.
Wherefore let him that thinketh he standeth take heed lest he fall.
Jas 4:15
For that ye ought to say, If the Lord will, we shall live, and do this, or that.
And all this assembly shall know that the LORD saveth not with sword and spear: for the battle is the LORD'S, and he will give you into our hands.
corruption_summary: "Nah, I’d win" is the boast that girds on the armor; the meme itself proves Scripture’s verdict that pride goeth before a fall.
corruption_paragraphs: Children enjoy the meme as irony, and the irony is wholesome — it laughs at the boaster who fell. The danger is when the joke becomes a posture: a self-confidence that never considers weakness, never says "if the Lord will," never asks for help. The culture rewards that posture; Scripture warns it.

Teach the two kinds of confidence. Gojo trusted his own strength and fell; David trusted the LORD and stood. Let your child be bold, and let his boldness have God as its object. Then teach him to brag, if at all, after the fight — and even then to say "thanks be to God."
roots_summary: Jujutsu Kaisen ch. 221 (Gojo: "Nah, I’d win," 2023) → Gojo’s defeat (ch. 236, September 2023) → overconfidence meme.
roots_lines: 2018-: Gege Akutami’s manga Jujutsu Kaisen
2023: chapter 221 — "Nah, I’d win"
September 2023: chapter 236 — Gojo’s defeat
Meme: impossible matchup + "nah, I’d win"
usage: "Could you eat ten hot dogs?" "Nah, I’d win." (He could not.)
Let not him that girdeth on his harness boast as he that putteth it off (1Ki 20:11).
Not "nah, I’d win," but "the battle is the LORD’s" (1Sa 17:47).

etymology: From the climax of the manga Jujutsu Kaisen (2023), where the demon king Sukuna, speaking to the sorcerer Gojo Satoru during their fight, says, "Stand proud, you are strong." The villain’s condescending praise became a meme template — "Stand proud, you’re strong" — used ironically to compliment someone who has just failed, or a small thing that tried hard, and Gen Alpha uses it as a mock-solemn salute.
biblical_def: "Stand proud, you’re strong" is a meme line from an anime villain, said to the hero he was beating. Gen Alpha kids say it as a joking compliment — to a little brother who lost at a game, to a dog who caught a ball. The Christian observation: the line holds two words Scripture handles with great care: proud and strong. Pride, in the Bible, is never something to stand in: "Every one that is proud in heart is an abomination to the LORD" (Pro 16:5), and "God resisteth the proud, and giveth grace to the humble" (1Pe 5:5). There is a right kind of glorying, and it is glorying in God: "let him that glorieth glory in this, that he understandeth and knoweth me" (Jer 9:24). And Christian strength is upside down: the Lord told Paul, "My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness," so that Paul could say, "when I am weak, then am I strong" (2Co 12:9-10). The villain praises strength from the top; Christ gives strength to the weak. A father can tell a five-year-old: "We don’t stand proud — we stand humble, and God makes us strong. Even when you lose, you’re strong if God is with you."
webster_summary: Sukuna’s condescending praise to Gojo in Jujutsu Kaisen (2023), now an ironic salute — a line about pride and strength that Scripture turns over: God resists the proud and perfects strength in weakness.
webster_full: STAND PROUD, phr. (manga meme, 2023–present; Gen Alpha usage) Ironic, mock-solemn praise, usually for one who lost or tried hard. "You came in last, but stand proud — you’re strong."
Source: Sukuna to Gojo, Jujutsu Kaisen (2023).
Decode for parents: playful irony; a door to talking about pride and strength.
Webster 1828, the root — PROUD, a. Having inordinate self-esteem; possessing a high or unreasonable conceit of one’s own excellence, either of body or mind.
scriptures: Pro 16:5
Every one that is proud in heart is an abomination to the LORD: though hand join in hand, he shall not be unpunished.
Likewise, ye younger, submit yourselves unto the elder. Yea, all of you be subject one to another, and be clothed with humility: for God resisteth the proud, and giveth grace to the humble.
Jer 9:24

But let him that glorieth glory in this, that he understandeth and knoweth me, that I am the LORD which exercise lovingkindness, judgment, and righteousness, in the earth: for in these things I delight, saith the LORD.

And he said unto me, My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness. Most gladly therefore will I rather glory in my infirmities, that the power of Christ may rest upon me.
Therefore I take pleasure in infirmities, in reproaches, in necessities, in persecutions, in distresses for Christ's sake: for when I am weak, then am I strong.
corruption_summary: "Stand proud" is a villain’s praise of strength from above; Scripture says God resists the proud and makes His strength perfect in weakness.
corruption_paragraphs: The meme is mostly harmless irony. But it lightly blesses a word Scripture treats as deadly. Our culture tells children to be proud — of themselves, of their identity, of their wins — and the Bible names pride as the root sin that cast down the devil. A meme that teaches "stand proud" as the highest compliment is a small catechism in the culture’s virtue.

Give your child the gospel inversion. The Christian stands humble and is lifted up (1Pe 5:6); he boasts in his weakness, and Christ’s power rests on him. When your son loses and someone jokes "stand proud," teach him the better line: "when I am weak, then am I strong."
roots_summary: Old English prud (proud, from Old French prud, valiant) → Jujutsu Kaisen "Stand proud, you are strong" (2023) → ironic Gen Alpha salute.
roots_lines: Late Old English prud — arrogant, haughty (from Old French prud, brave)
2023: Sukuna’s line to Gojo in Jujutsu Kaisen
Meme template: "Stand proud, you’re strong"
Gen Alpha: ironic praise for the defeated
usage: "You fell off the scooter — stand proud, you’re strong."
God resisteth the proud, and giveth grace to the humble (1Pe 5:5).
When I am weak, then am I strong — the Christian version (2Co 12:10).

etymology: Son Goku, the hero of Akira Toriyama’s Dragon Ball manga (1984–95) and its anime series, above all Dragon Ball Z (1989–96); the character is loosely based on Sun Wukong, the Monkey King of the Chinese classic Journey to the West. Goku’s ever-escalating power levels and transformations (Super Saiyan and beyond) made him the playground benchmark of strength — "It’s over 9000!" (a 2006 meme from the English dub) and endless "Could Goku beat ___?" debates. Toriyama died in March 2024, and a new generation still argues power-scaling.
biblical_def: To Gen Alpha, Goku is the ultimate strong guy — the anime hero who keeps getting more powerful. "Who would win, Goku or ___?" is a playground argument that never ends, and sometimes a child asks, "Could Goku beat Jesus?" The Christian observation: the question is a good one to answer, because it lets a father explain who Jesus is. Goku is a cartoon character, drawn by a man; Jesus is the Lord who made everything: "For by him were all things created, that are in heaven, and that are in earth, visible and invisible" (Col 1:16). After His resurrection He said, "All power is given unto me in heaven and in earth" (Mat 28:18). There is no power level above His. But the most astonishing thing about Jesus’s power is how He used it. He "made himself of no reputation, and took upon him the form of a servant... and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross" (Php 2:7-8). Goku powers up to win fights; Christ laid His power down to save enemies. And His strength is for the weak: "He giveth power to the faint; and to them that have no might he increaseth strength" (Isa 40:29). A father can tell a five-year-old: "Goku is a pretend hero. Jesus is real, and He’s stronger than anyone — He made the whole universe! And He uses His power to help and save us."
webster_summary: Dragon Ball‘s hero (Toriyama, 1984-) and the playground benchmark of power — a cartoon strongman who lets a father explain the One with all power, who laid it down to save.
webster_full: GOKU, proper n. (anime hero, Dragon Ball, 1984–present; Gen Alpha usage) Son Goku; by extension, the benchmark of overwhelming power. "He’s basically Goku at dodgeball."
Related memes: "It’s over 9000!" (2006), Super Saiyan, power-scaling debates.
Based loosely on Sun Wukong, the Monkey King of Journey to the West.
Decode for parents: action-cartoon violence; a great opening for "who is really strongest?"
scriptures: Col 1:16

For by him were all things created, that are in heaven, and that are in earth, visible and invisible, whether they be thrones, or dominions, or principalities, or powers: all things were created by him, and for him:
And Jesus came and spake unto them, saying, All power is given unto me in heaven and in earth.
Php 2:7
But made himself of no reputation, and took upon him the form of a servant, and was made in the likeness of men:
Php 2:8
And being found in fashion as a man, he humbled himself, and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross.
He giveth power to the faint; and to them that have no might he increaseth strength.
corruption_summary: Goku is harmless as a cartoon; the power-worship of the playground debate is answered by the Christ who has all power and used it as a servant.
corruption_paragraphs: Power fantasies are an old part of boyhood, and Dragon Ball is one of the most influential. Its moral world is simple: strength grows by training and fighting, and the strongest wins. That is not wicked, but it is incomplete. A boy whose highest picture of greatness is the Super Saiyan has not yet seen the cross.

Use the debate. When your son asks who would win, tell him who made the universe, and then tell him what that Person did with His power. The meekness of Christ is not weakness; it is omnipotence choosing to serve.
roots_summary: Chinese Sun Wukong (Journey to the West, 16th c.) → Toriyama’s Son Goku (Dragon Ball, 1984) → Dragon Ball Z (1989–96) → power-scaling benchmark.

All power is given unto me in heaven and in earth (Mat 28:18).

etymology: From a May 2021 video the wrestler and actor John Cena posted to the Chinese social network Weibo, promoting a film in Mandarin while holding an ice-cream cone: "Zaoshang hao Zhongguo, xianzai wo you bingqilin" — "Good morning, China; now I have ice cream." Bingqilin (ice cream) sounds to English ears like "bing chilling," and the clip became a global meme in 2021–22. Gen Alpha uses "bing chilling" for ice cream, for relaxing ("just bing chilling"), and as a nonsense shout.
biblical_def: "Bing chilling" is a silly way to say ice cream — or to say you’re relaxing. It comes from a video of John Cena saying "ice cream" in Chinese. The Christian observation: there is nothing to fix in a joke about ice cream, and something to enjoy. Scripture says simple pleasures are gifts: God "giveth us richly all things to enjoy" (1Ti 6:17); "Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, and cometh down from the Father of lights" (Jas 1:17). The Preacher says that to "eat and drink, and enjoy the good of all his labour, it is the gift of God" (Ecc 3:13). An ice cream cone on a summer porch, a whole family laughing at a meme, a Saturday of "just chilling" — these are mercies. The only care is the ordinary one: rest is good when it follows work and leads to thanks (Exo 20:9-10), and dessert is good when it does not rule the belly (Pro 23:2). A father can tell a five-year-old: "Bing chilling! God made ice cream taste good because He loves to give us happy things. Let’s say thank You to Him before we eat it." Few slang words lead so directly to gratitude.
webster_summary: John Cena’s Mandarin "ice cream" (bingqilin) video of May 2021 — a harmless joke for ice cream and relaxing, and a nudge toward thanks for good gifts.
webster_full: BING CHILLING, phr. (internet meme, 2021–present; Gen Alpha usage) Ice cream; relaxing; a nonsense shout. "Just bing chilling on the couch."
From Mandarin bingqilin, ice cream, as said by John Cena (May 2021).
Decode for parents: completely harmless.
Webster 1828, the root — CHILL, n. A shivering with cold; rigors, as in an ague; the cold fit that precedes a fever; sensation of cold in an animal body; chilliness. [ See Cold and Heat .]
scriptures: Charge them that are rich in this world, that they be not highminded, nor trust in uncertain riches, but in the living God, who giveth us richly all things to enjoy;
Jas 1:17
Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, and cometh down from the Father of lights, with whom is no variableness, neither shadow of turning.
Ecc 3:13
And also that every man should eat and drink, and enjoy the good of all his labour, it is the gift of God.
Pro 23:2
And put a knife to thy throat, if thou be a man given to appetite.
corruption_summary: "Bing chilling" is innocent fun; its only caution is the ordinary one of rest without work and dessert without restraint.
corruption_paragraphs: There is almost nothing here to correct. The meme is cross-cultural silliness, and laughter is a gift. If anything, "just chilling" as a life motto can drift toward the sluggard’s love of ease (Pro 6:9-10), but that is a caution about habits, not the word.
Enjoy it and add thanks. A family that says grace over ice cream is teaching that every good thing comes from the Father. Let the meme be a reminder: God gives us richly all things to enjoy.
roots_summary: Mandarin bingqilin (ice cream) → John Cena’s Weibo video (May 2021) → global meme "bing chilling" (2021–22).
roots_lines: Mandarin bing (ice) + qilin (from English "cream") → bingqilin, ice cream
May 2021: John Cena’s Mandarin promotional video
2021–22: global meme; "bing chilling" as ice cream and relaxing
English chill — cold; slang: to relax
usage: "Can we get bing chilling after the game?"
God giveth us richly all things to enjoy — including bing chilling (1Ti 6:17).
Every good gift is from above — say thanks for the cone (Jas 1:17).

etymology: A meme genre that exploded on TikTok in early 2025: AI-generated images of absurd hybrid creatures — a shark in sneakers, a crocodile-bomber plane, a log with a baseball bat, a ballerina with a cappuccino-cup head — given pseudo-Italian (and some Indonesian) names and narrated by a text-to-speech voice in rhyming Italian-sounding nonsense. Characters such as Tralalero Tralala, Bombardiro Crocodilo, Tung Tung Tung Sahur, Ballerina Cappuccina, and Brr Brr Patapim became Gen Alpha celebrities, then Roblox games (Steal a Brainrot), toys, and trading cards. Several of the original voice-overs carried Italian blasphemies and crude or violent jokes that children repeat without understanding them.
biblical_def: Italian brainrot is the 2025 craze of silly AI-made creatures with fake-Italian names — Tralalero Tralala, Tung Tung Tung Sahur, Ballerina Cappuccina — that Gen Alpha kids collect, quote, and chant. Much of it is plain nonsense. The Christian observation: two things make this more than nonsense. First, several of the original audio chants contain blasphemies against God in Italian, and children who chant them are taking the Lord’s name in vain without knowing it. The Third Commandment does not have an exception for languages we do not speak: "Thou shalt not take the name of the LORD thy God in vain; for the LORD will not hold him guiltless that taketh his name in vain" (Exo 20:7). Second, the whole genre is "brainrot" by its own name — content built to be mindless and endlessly repeatable. Jesus said, "every idle word that men shall speak, they shall give account thereof in the day of judgment" (Mat 12:36), and Paul gives the antidote: "whatsoever things are true... think on these things" (Php 4:8). A father can tell a five-year-old: "Some of those funny songs have bad words about God hidden in them, in another language. We love God’s name, so we don’t sing those. Let’s make up our own silly animal songs instead!" Silliness is fine; blasphemy is not, even in a costume.
webster_summary: 2025 AI-meme genre of absurd pseudo-Italian creatures (Tralalero Tralala and company), some of whose original chants blaspheme God in Italian — brainrot by name and, in places, the Third Commandment broken in a costume.
webster_full: ITALIAN BRAINROT, n. (TikTok meme genre, early 2025–present; Gen Alpha) AI-generated absurd creatures with pseudo-Italian names and TTS chants; the characters and the craze. "Who’s your favorite Italian brainrot?"
Characters in kid lore: Tralalero Tralala, Bombardiro Crocodilo, Tung Tung Tung Sahur, Ballerina Cappuccina, Brr Brr Patapim, Lirili Larila, Chimpanzini Bananini.
Spread to Roblox (Steal a Brainrot), toys, and trading cards.
Decode for parents: the images are silly; several original audios contain Italian blasphemy and crude or violent lines — check what your child is chanting.
scriptures: Exo 20:7
Thou shalt not take the name of the LORD thy God in vain; for the LORD will not hold him guiltless that taketh his name in vain.
But I say unto you, That every idle word that men shall speak, they shall give account thereof in the day of judgment.
Php 4:8

Finally, brethren, whatsoever things are true, whatsoever things are honest, whatsoever things are just, whatsoever things are pure, whatsoever things are lovely, whatsoever things are of good report; if there be any virtue, and if there be any praise, think on these things.
Eph 5:4
Neither filthiness, nor foolish talking, nor jesting, which are not convenient: but rather giving of thanks.
corruption_summary: Italian brainrot is engineered nonsense, and some of its chants smuggle blasphemy and crude violence past children who cannot understand them; Scripture guards the Name and calls every idle word to account.
corruption_paragraphs: The genre’s appeal is its meaninglessness: random creatures, rhythmic nonsense, endless remixes. Children love it the way they love any silly chant. But meaning hides in the noise. Some of the most famous original voice-overs include Italian oaths against God, and others joke crudely about bombings; a child who repeats them is saying things he would be horrified to understand. Ignorance lessens guilt, but it does not make the words clean.

Reject the originals; redeem the impulse. Children are made to delight in silly sounds and strange creatures — God made the ostrich and the leviathan. Give them that delight cleanly: invent family creatures with funny names, read them Job 39 and 41, and keep God’s name holy in every language.
roots_summary: Italian-sounding nonsense names + AI images + TTS chants (TikTok, January 2025) → Gen Alpha character craze → Roblox, toys, cards.
roots_lines: Brainrot — Gen-Z term for mind-numbing content (2020s)
January 2025: Tralalero Tralala and the first AI-creature chants on TikTok
Spring 2025: Bombardiro Crocodilo, Tung Tung Tung Sahur (Indonesian), Ballerina Cappuccina, and dozens more
Summer 2025: Steal a Brainrot (Roblox), merchandise, trading cards
usage: "Tung tung tung tung SAHUR!" "Do you know what the Tralalero one actually says?"
The LORD will not hold him guiltless that taketh his name in vain — in any language (Exo 20:7).
Every idle word — even Italian nonsense — shall give account (Mat 12:36).

etymology: McDonald’s purple, berry-flavored milkshake, sold from June 12, 2023, for the birthday of Grimace, the round purple mascot introduced in 1971 (originally as the four-armed "Evil Grimace" who stole milkshakes). Within days a TikTok trend took over: a creator wishes Grimace a happy birthday, sips the shake, and the clip cuts to a staged horror scene — the person collapsed, "dead," or possessed, splattered with purple. Millions of copies followed, and "Grimace shake" became shorthand for a cursed object or a comic-horror twist.
biblical_def: The Grimace shake was a purple McDonald’s milkshake, and the 2023 TikTok joke was that drinking it made you "die" — people filmed themselves taking a sip and then lying in a heap, covered in purple. Gen Alpha still calls something weird or dangerous a "Grimace shake." The Christian observation: the trend is comic horror, and much of it is just goofy. But it is goofy about death, and children absorbed a joke that death is a punchline and a prop. Scripture is not grim about death, but it is sober: "It is better to go to the house of mourning, than to go to the house of feasting: for that is the end of all men; and the living will lay it to his heart" (Ecc 7:2). Moses prayed, "So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom" (Psa 90:12). The Christian can laugh at death only for one reason — because Christ has defeated it: "O death, where is thy sting? O grave, where is thy victory?" (1Co 15:55). Jesus came to "deliver them who through fear of death were all their lifetime subject to bondage" (Heb 2:15). A father can tell a five-year-old: "That was a pretend joke. Real dying is sad, but Jesus beat death, so people who love Him live forever with Him. That’s why we’re not afraid."
webster_summary: McDonald’s purple birthday shake (June 2023) and the TikTok trend of staged "deaths" after a sip — comic horror that made death a prop, against Scripture’s sober and victorious view of the grave.
webster_full: GRIMACE SHAKE, n. (McDonald’s, June 2023; TikTok trend) The purple birthday milkshake; the meme of a sip followed by a staged horror "death"; anything cursed. "Don’t drink that, it’s a Grimace shake."
Grimace: McDonald’s mascot since 1971 (first as "Evil Grimace").
Decode for parents: mostly silly; some younger children found the clips genuinely frightening.

Webster 1828, the root — SHAKE, v.t. To cause to move with quick vibrations; to move rapidly one way and the other; to agitate; as, the wind shakes a tree; an earthquake shakes the hills or the earth.
scriptures: Ecc 7:2
It is better to go to the house of mourning, than to go to the house of feasting: for that is the end of all men; and the living will lay it to his heart.
So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom.
O death, where is thy sting? O grave, where is thy victory?
Heb 2:15
And deliver them who through fear of death were all their lifetime subject to bondage.
corruption_summary: The Grimace-shake trend treated death as a slapstick prop; Scripture is sober about death and laughs at it only from the far side of the empty tomb.
corruption_paragraphs: Gallows humor is old, and the trend was mostly harmless theater. Its deeper effect is cultural: a generation that rarely sees real death sees thousands of comic fake ones. Death becomes unserious, a gag for views, and the sobriety Ecclesiastes commends — laying the end of all men to heart — grows harder.

Use the meme to talk about death plainly. Children are curious and often afraid. Tell them death is real and sad, that it came by sin, and that Jesus has defeated it. Then Christians can laugh at death the way Paul did — "where is thy sting?" — not because it is a joke, but because it has lost.
roots_summary: English grimace (a twisted face; French) → McDonald’s mascot Grimace (1971) → Grimace Birthday shake (June 2023) → TikTok staged-death trend.

1971: McDonaldland’s "Evil Grimace," the shake thief; later the friendly purple Grimace
June 12, 2023: Grimace Birthday Meal and shake
June 2023: TikTok trend — a sip, then a staged horror scene
usage: "That cafeteria milk looks like a Grimace shake."
Teach us to number our days — even the meme-ish ones (Psa 90:12).
O death, where is thy sting? — the only reason we can laugh (1Co 15:55).

etymology: From tweak (to pinch or twist, sixteenth century) through 1990s American drug slang, where a tweaker is a methamphetamine user and tweaking the jittery, paranoid behavior of a high. By the 2010s hip-hop and internet usage had widened tweakin’ to mean acting irrationally, overreacting, or being wrong, and the reaction phrase "nahh, he tweakin’" — often over a video of someone’s bizarre take — spread through TikTok and Twitch around 2021. Gen Alpha uses it for anyone saying or doing something ridiculous.
biblical_def: "Nahh, he tweakin’" means "No way — he’s acting crazy," said when someone says something ridiculous or overreacts. Gen Alpha kids say it about classmates, streamers, siblings, and sometimes their parents. The Christian observation: parents should know where the word comes from. "Tweaking" was first slang for the jittery, paranoid behavior of a methamphetamine addict — a real misery that has destroyed many families. The children using it today do not mean that, but the word carries a sneer at someone’s mind. Scripture urges two kinds of care with words like this. The first is care in judging: "He that answereth a matter before he heareth it, it is folly and shame unto him" (Pro 18:13), and "Speak not evil one of another, brethren" (Jas 4:11). Calling someone crazy is a quick way to dismiss him without listening. The second is compassion for those who truly are bound: the body is "the temple of the Holy Ghost" (1Co 6:19), and Christ came "to preach deliverance to the captives" (Luk 4:18) — including the ones the slang mocks. A father can tell a five-year-old: "When someone says something silly, we don’t call them crazy. We listen first, and then we can say, ‘I don’t think that’s right.’" He can tell the older child where the word started, and pray for those it first described.
webster_summary: Reaction phrase (c. 2021) from 1990s meth slang tweaker, now "he’s acting crazy" — a quick dismissal Scripture slows down, and a root that calls for compassion rather than a sneer.
webster_full: NAHH, HE TWEAKIN’, phr. (internet slang, c. 2021–present; Gen Alpha) "He is acting crazy / overreacting / wrong." "He said pineapple belongs on cereal — nahh, he tweakin’."
Tweakin’ — acting irrationally; from 1990s drug slang tweaker, a methamphetamine user.
Variants: you tweakin’, stop tweakin’.
Decode for parents: children rarely know the drug root; tell them, and teach them to listen before dismissing.
scriptures: He that answereth a matter before he heareth it, it is folly and shame unto him.
Jas 4:11

Speak not evil one of another, brethren. He that speaketh evil of his brother, and judgeth his brother, speaketh evil of the law, and judgeth the law: but if thou judge the law, thou art not a doer of the law, but a judge.
What? know ye not that your body is the temple of the Holy Ghost which is in you, which ye have of God, and ye are not your own?
Luk 4:18

The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he hath anointed me to preach the gospel to the poor; he hath sent me to heal the brokenhearted, to preach deliverance to the captives, and recovering of sight to the blind, to set at liberty them that are bruised,
corruption_summary: "He tweakin’" dismisses a neighbor as unhinged, in a word borrowed from the misery of addiction; Scripture slows the judgment and sends compassion to the captives.
corruption_paragraphs: Slang often launders suffering into jokes. "Tweaking" began as a description of people in the grip of a ruinous drug, and it now names a classmate’s odd opinion. The children using it mean no harm, but the habit is a reflex of contempt — the other person is crazy, so I need not listen.

Teach the slower response. Hear before answering; disagree without dismissing. And when the word comes up, tell your child about addiction, and about the deliverance Christ brings. A word used to sneer at the broken can become a reason to pray for them.
roots_summary: Old English twiccian (to pluck) → tweak → 1990s drug slang tweaker / tweaking → internet "nahh, he tweakin’" (c. 2021).

2010s hip-hop and internet: tweakin’, acting irrationally

usage: "He thinks the moon is fake. Nahh, he tweakin’." "Or maybe ask him why first."
He that answereth a matter before he heareth it, it is folly (Pro 18:13).
Christ came to preach deliverance to the captives — even the ones the slang mocks (Luk 4:18).

etymology: A caption formula that spread on TikTok and Instagram around 2022: "Bro thinks he’s [a superhero / a chef / the main character]" posted under a clip of someone (or some animal) acting more impressive than he is. The variant "bro thinks he’s him" (from "he’s him," he’s the man) mocks self-importance in general. Gen Alpha says it out loud about classmates, siblings, and pets — "bro thinks he’s a lion" of a cat stalking a leaf.
biblical_def: "Bro thinks he’s ___" is a way to poke fun at someone acting bigger than he is: "Bro thinks he’s a pro," "Bro thinks he’s him." Gen Alpha kids say it about friends, brothers, and the family cat. The Christian observation: the phrase mocks pride, and Scripture also exposes pride — but it aims first at the mirror. "For if a man think himself to be something, when he is nothing, he deceiveth himself" (Gal 6:3). Paul told every believer "not to think of himself more highly than he ought to think" (Rom 12:3). The Pharisee in Jesus’s parable was a perfect "bro thinks he’s": "God, I thank thee, that I am not as other men are" (Luk 18:11). But notice the trap: the Pharisee was mocking the publican’s lowliness. A child who mocks others’ pretension can be doing the very same thing. Jesus asks, "why beholdest thou the mote that is in thy brother’s eye, but considerest not the beam that is in thine own eye?" (Mat 7:3). A father can tell a five-year-old: "It’s funny when the cat thinks he’s a lion! But we don’t make fun of people for showing off. We ask God to help us not think we’re bigger than we are." The best use of the phrase is on yourself.
webster_summary: Caption formula (c. 2022) mocking pretension — "bro thinks he’s him" — which Scripture sharpens: pride deceives itself, and the mocker of the mote must mind the beam.
webster_full: BRO THINKS HE’S, phr. (internet caption formula, c. 2022–present; Gen Alpha) A teasing frame mocking someone acting grander than he is. "Bro thinks he’s a ninja."
Bro thinks he’s him — he thinks he is the man, the star.
Used of people, pets, and objects alike.
Decode for parents: mostly gentle teasing; it can sharpen into contempt.
scriptures: Gal 6:3
For if a man think himself to be something, when he is nothing, he deceiveth himself.
Rom 12:3

For I say, through the grace given unto me, to every man that is among you, not to think of himself more highly than he ought to think; but to think soberly, according as God hath dealt to every man the measure of faith.
The Pharisee stood and prayed thus with himself, God, I thank thee, that I am not as other men are, extortioners, unjust, adulterers, or even as this publican.
Mat 7:3
And why beholdest thou the mote that is in thy brother's eye, but considerest not the beam that is in thine own eye?
corruption_summary: "Bro thinks he’s" mocks another’s pretension and can itself be a Pharisee’s sneer; Scripture turns the joke inward — the self-deceived are many, and the beam is in my own eye.
corruption_paragraphs: Much of this is harmless ribbing; families tease, and teasing can be affectionate. But the formula’s engine is contempt for pretension, and contempt is easy to aim and hard to aim honestly. A culture of constant mockery makes children afraid to try anything earnest, lest someone caption them.

Teach the mirror. Laugh at the cat, then ask: where do I think I’m "him"? Make humility the family’s shared joke — the father who laughs at himself first teaches his children that pride is funny because it is false, not because others have it.
roots_summary: Bro (brother) + "thinks he’s" → TikTok caption formula (c. 2022) → "bro thinks he’s him."

"He’s him" — he’s the man; hence "bro thinks he’s him"
Gen Alpha: said aloud of people and pets
usage: "Bro thinks he’s a lion" (of the cat, stalking a leaf).
If a man think himself to be something when he is nothing, he deceiveth himself (Gal 6:3).
